newsitem.title: CHINA: Deng family hamlet becomes Mecca for mourners.
newsitem.headline: Deng family hamlet becomes Mecca for mourners.

text.p: The death of Deng Xiaoping has turned a dot on the map into a teeming Mecca as hundreds of thousands of mourners make pilgrimages to his hometown to pay their respects to the late paramount leader.
Weeping crowds have thronged the tiny village of Paifang in the southwestern province of Sichuan since Thursday morning, when Deng's death at 92 the previous night was announced.

Some of the grieving had travelled from Hong Kong, 1,150 km (715 miles) away, or even Taiwan, about 1,650 (1,000 miles) distant, said an official with the Deng Xiaoping Former Residence Management Office that tends the old Deng family estate.
"Up through today more than 200,000 people have come," the official said by telephone.

"The courtyard and the surrounding area are filled with people, people are wearing white flowers and black veils," the official said. "There is an endless flow of people in here, the lines are reaching into the streets."

Deng's old courtyard abode, where a makeshift shrine has been set up for mourners to pay their last respects to the mastermind of China's economic boom, has thrown open its doors 24 hours a day to handle the flood of visitors.
"There are about one or two hundred people keeping order, including the People's Armed Police and volunteer groups organised by the masses," the official said.

Mourners were limited to visits of three minutes to ensure everyone got a chance to honour the diminutive reformer whose market-oriented policies gave Chinese the green light to make money after years of poverty under Mao Zedong.
"Many people are crying, and those weeping so bitterly they don't leave and have to be ushered out," the official said.
"From the looks of things there will be even more people in the next few days. The numbers of people are growing day by day," he said.
Public expressions of grief in Paifang for Deng's passing were in contrast to the capital Beijing, where authorities have clamped down on unauthorised displays of mourning.
